ONE SEGMENT, ONE COSTING PER BOOKING — and that is the whole point.
These bookings used to carry a flight AND a hotel. On 10-Aug-2026 that shape
killed a real TravelPay run: all three receipts came back
Allocation cannot be greater than Amount Received
because the receipt was raised for the COSTING's fare while `allocation:
"ALL"` clicks Tramada's Select All, which ticks EVERY allocatable row —
the hotel as well. Booking 13199 was receipted for 200.00 and Select All
allocated 200.00 + 60.00. Booking 13202 was receipted for 250.00 and Select
All allocated 250.00 + 790.00. Tramada was right to refuse both.
A flight segment produces no allocatable row of its own — its ticket costing
does. So one flight + one ticket costing = exactly ONE row on the receipt
form, worth exactly the fare. Select All then cannot exceed the receipt, by
construction rather than by arithmetic that has to stay in step.
Keep it that way. If a booking ever needs a hotel as well, the receipt has
to be raised for the SUM of every allocatable row, or allocate explicitly
instead of "ALL" — see make-fixtures.js `costedCents`.
THE SMALL END-TO-END TEST
node make-fixtures.js travelpay --limit 1
THE AMOUNTS ARE CHOSEN, NOT ARBITRARY.
With arbitrary fares every row of a run comes back "Not allocated" and
the run demonstrates nothing. Against statement-rows.json's six rows —
three fares produce all three outcomes:
booking 1  fare 145.54
row 1  150.00  -> settles the fare, 4.46 left over   Part allocated
row 4  145.54  -> nothing left outstanding           Not allocated
booking 2  fare 200.00
row 2  200.00  -> settles the fare exactly           Allocated
row 5  100.00  -> nothing left outstanding           Not allocated
booking 3  fare 790.00
row 3  200.00  -> nothing is small enough            Not allocated
row 6  790.00  -> settles the fare exactly           Allocated
test-recon-core.js asserts that pairing, because it is a property of two
files that can quietly drift apart.
clientCode must already exist in Tramada (SURNAME/FIRSTNAME), and creditor
must be a real Tramada creditor — an unmatched one stops the run and asks.
THE CLIENT HERE IS A FALLBACK — make-fixtures.js CHOOSES IT PER REPORT
See CLIENT_FOR in make-fixtures.js: bpay builds under GRAY/MEGAN, the
other three under GRAY/SPIDER, and --client overrides either. The value
below is only used for a report that table has no opinion about.
The difference decides whether a BPay receipt can be raised at all.
The booking Receipts page's #receiptCategory
dropdown offers the DEBTOR variants when the client is a debtor account and
the CLIENT variants when it is a retail one — the two lists never overlap:
13115  GRAY/MEGAN DR   Debtor Payment Receipt, Agency CC Debtor Receipt,
Migration Debtor Payment Receipt, Creditor Refund
13394  GRAY/SPIDER MS  Client Payment Receipt, Agency CC Client Receipt,
Migration Client Payment Receipt, Creditor Refund
Both bookings carry the same DEBTOR (RAA of SA Limited (Retail)); it is the
CLIENT's account type that swaps the list. A BPay payment belongs on a
debtor-account booking, so BPay fixtures built under GRAY/SPIDER can never
exercise steps 11 or 30 — the run stops every row with "Please review,
Debtor Payment Receipt not available", correctly.
It runs the other way too: TravelPay CHECKS receipts filtered to Client
Payment Receipt, so ITS fixtures must be built under a retail client or
the receipts it seeds are a type its own run never looks at.
